text: In Nairobi slums, women often discontinue DMPA injectables due to irregular bleeding and fear of infertility rumors. Community health workers report that counseling on expected side effects improves continuation rates.
Implant removal requires a trained provider. Women in informal settlements cite transport cost and long clinic waits as barriers to removal when experiencing heavy bleeding.

Reversing the stall in fertility decline: stock-outs of combined oral contraceptives at public facilities were associated with method switching to condoms or discontinuation entirely in peri-urban Kenya.
Unwanted pregnancy in Nairobi slums: progestogen-only pills were preferred among breastfeeding mothers who feared combined pill effects on milk supply, though daily adherence remained challenging.
Copper IUD uptake is low in some slum clinics due to pain during insertion and myths about IUDs and infertility. Peer educator programs increased acceptance when side effects were explained.
Male partner objection remains a leading reason for contraceptive non-use among young women in Nairobi informal settlements, even when methods are available at no cost.
In Kampala peri-urban areas, weight gain and amenorrhea were commonly reported reasons for injectable discontinuation; women often switched to implants or pills without clinic guidance.
APHRC findings note emergency contraception is underused in slums despite high unwanted pregnancy rates, largely due to lack of awareness and stigma at pharmacy level.
